texts.0: SP, due to prolonged head-down time on the GPS control panel, interrupted the instrument and outside crosscheck and did not hold the briefed navigation altitude. The excursion exceeded 300 feet and continued to develop unnoticed while data entry went on. The IP had to direct the return to the assigned altitude before the next turning point.
texts.1: SP, due to task saturation while sequencing the GPS flight plan, released altitude control and allowed the aircraft to settle. The deviation reached about 300 feet and stabilized only at the limit of tolerance. Recovery followed repeated verbal prompting from the IP rather than SP's own crosscheck.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow scan pattern while selecting GPS pages, allowed the navigation altitude to drift between 150 and 300 feet. SP detected the trend on the altimeter and returned to the briefed altitude in good time without IP input. The excursion was contained, although the pitch correction was larger than required.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation altitude within 150 feet throughout GPS programming and monitoring. Head-down periods were kept short and each one was closed with an immediate altimeter check. Corrections were small, prompt and made with smooth pitch and power inputs.
texts.4: SP held the briefed navigation altitude with negligible deviation while working the GPS. Altimeter checks were interleaved with every page selection, so no drift was allowed to build. Aircraft control remained precise and entirely unaffected by the equipment workload.
texts.marginal: SP remained within altitude standards, but every GPS entry produced a repeatable sag of about 100 feet that was corrected only after several seconds. The trend was consistent and grew with the length of the head-down period. SP is expected to shorten the interruption of the altimeter crosscheck so that altitude holding does not depend on the GPS workload.

texts_at.0: With the IP monitoring the altimeter and calling the correction needed while SP entered the GPS flight plan, SP adjusted the altitude on the call given. Interleaving the altimeter crosscheck with GPS page selection independently has not yet been asked of SP, so altitude control during GPS work still depends on the IP's call at this stage. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin glancing at the altimeter once during every GPS entry, with the IP still calling any excursion missed, before independent altitude control during GPS operation is required.
texts_at.1: SP returned to the briefed navigation altitude with the excursion at about 280 feet before the trend was fully arrested. The delay traced to the GPS flight plan being sequenced without a break in the altimeter crosscheck on the earliest pages worked. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to break off the GPS sequencing at a fixed interval and confirm the altimeter before continuing, from the first page onward.
texts_at.2: SP detected the trend on the altimeter and returned to the briefed altitude, holding the excursion to about 210 feet. The drift traced to a scan pattern that slowed while selecting GPS pages rather than staying interleaved with the altimeter. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to interleave the altimeter check with every GPS page selection, not only after several pages have been worked.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation altitude within about 95 feet throughout GPS programming and monitoring. The small residual came from a head-down period closed a moment later than the earliest point it could have been. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to close every head-down period a moment earlier so the residual altitude drift is removed.

texts_above.1: SP adjusted the altitude on the correction called by the IP, holding the excursion to about 280 feet from the assigned value before the trend was arrested. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP interleaved the altimeter crosscheck with the GPS page selections, holding the excursion to about 200 feet throughout the programming task. Closing each head-down period a moment earlier still would tighten that margin further on a longer entry. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control during GPS operation.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation altitude within about 95 feet throughout GPS programming and monitoring, with head-down periods kept short and each one closed with an immediate altimeter check. The technique is already sound; only the longest waypoint entries still call for the check to be a shade quicker. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude discipline under GPS workload.
texts_above.4: SP held the briefed navigation altitude with the deviation inside about 30 feet while working the GPS, with altimeter checks interleaved into every page selection. The only refinement available was to log the interleave rhythm used for the debrief, since altitude control itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude control under GPS workload.

texts.0: SP, due to inattention to power setting while entering GPS waypoint data, did not maintain the briefed navigation airspeed. The excursion passed 20 knots and left the aircraft off the planned timing to the next turning point. The IP had to call for the power correction to restore the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to reset power after a GPS-driven turn, allowed the airspeed to decay to the 20 knot limit. The value settled at the edge of tolerance and was corrected only after direct verbal cueing. SP's own crosscheck did not capture the error.
texts.2: SP, due to delayed power adjustment during GPS page management, allowed airspeed to vary between 10 and 20 knots from the briefed figure. SP identified the deviation and restored the target speed without IP intervention. Timing to the next turning point was preserved.
texts.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation airspeed within 10 knots while operating the GPS. Power was set and trimmed before each head-down task, so the speed stayed stable. Ground speed and estimated times to the turning points remained consistent with the plan.
texts.4: SP held the briefed navigation airspeed with negligible variation across the whole GPS workload. Power management was anticipatory, with adjustments made before the speed could move. Timing accuracy at each turning point matched the flight plan exactly.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside airspeed standards but consistently ran near the low end of the tolerance while head-down on the GPS. Each correction was late and required a noticeable power increase. SP is expected to set and verify power before starting any GPS entry so that airspeed control stops trailing the equipment task.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the power correction needed after a GPS-driven turn, SP applied the power change called. Resetting power for the navigation airspeed independently after a GPS-driven turn has not yet been asked of SP, so airspeed control during GPS work still depends on the IP's call at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin including the airspeed indicator in the scan once during every GPS-driven turn, with the IP still calling the power change needed, before independent airspeed control is required.
texts_at.1: SP restored the briefed navigation airspeed with the deviation at about 18 knots before the leg timing was affected. The delay traced to power left unreset after a GPS-driven turn on the earliest legs of the route. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reset power immediately after every GPS-driven turn, from the first one of the route.
texts_at.2: SP identified the deviation and restored the target speed, holding the excursion to about 14 knots from the briefed value. The delay traced to a power adjustment left for after the GPS page management rather than made during it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to adjust power during the page management itself, not after it is complete.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation airspeed within about 6 knots while operating the GPS. The small residual came from a trim check completed a moment after the head-down task rather than before it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the trim check before, not after, each head-down GPS task.

texts_above.1: SP applied the power change called by the IP, restoring the briefed navigation airspeed with the deviation held to about 18 knots before the leg timing was affected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP set and trimmed power before each head-down GPS task, holding the airspeed deviation to about 15 knots throughout. Completing that trim check before the task rather than reacting after it would tighten the margin further on the next entry. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound airspeed control during GPS operation.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the briefed navigation airspeed within about 6 knots while operating the GPS, with power set and trimmed before each head-down task. The technique is already sound; only the longest waypoint entries still call for the trim check to be made a moment sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed airspeed management under GPS workload.
texts_above.4: SP held the briefed navigation airspeed with the deviation inside about 2 knots across the whole GPS workload, with power management anticipatory throughout. The only refinement available was to log the power settings used for the debrief, since airspeed control itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional airspeed control during GPS operation.

error_modes.label: Heading and course tracking to the active waypoint

texts.0: SP, due to uncoordinated inputs while reading the GPS course window, did not fly the computed course to the active waypoint. Heading error exceeded 10 degrees and the track offset kept increasing toward the turning point. The IP had to take corrective action to regain the planned route.
texts.1: SP, due to chasing the GPS course deviation indicator instead of flying a steady heading, oscillated on either side of the computed course and reached the 10 degree limit. The heading was stabilized only after IP prompting. Cross-track error at the turning point was clearly visible.
texts.2: SP, due to a late response to a small drift, allowed heading error to grow to between 5 and 10 degrees from the computed course. SP recognized the divergence on the HSI and re-established the course promptly without IP input. The turning point was still made on the planned track.
texts.3: SP flew the GPS computed course within 5 degrees on every leg. Heading corrections were small, coordinated and applied as soon as the course deviation moved. Each turning point was crossed on the planned track.
texts.4: SP tracked the GPS computed course with negligible heading error throughout the route. Drift corrections were anticipated rather than reactive, so the deviation indicator stayed centered. Turning point crossings required no late corrections.
texts.marginal: SP held heading within standards, but corrections to the computed course were repeatedly made as a series of small overshoots rather than a single input. The pattern appeared on every leg and cost track accuracy near the turning points. SP is expected to establish a drift-corrected heading and hold it instead of chasing the indicator.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the steady heading to hold instead of the course deviation indicator, SP flew the heading given rather than chasing the needle. Establishing a drift-corrected heading independently, rather than chasing the deviation indicator, has not yet been asked of SP, so course tracking still depends on the IP's call at this stage. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin naming the drift observed on the indicator before the IP calls the heading, with the IP still confirming it, before an independent heading is required.
texts_at.1: SP stabilized the heading on the computed course with the error at about 9 degrees before the oscillation stopped. The delay traced to the course deviation indicator being chased rather than a steady heading being flown on the earliest part of the leg. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to establish a drift-corrected heading and hold it from the first indication of drift, rather than chasing the indicator.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the divergence on the HSI and re-established the course promptly, holding the error to about 7 degrees from the computed course. The late response traced to a small drift that was allowed to build before the correction was applied. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to respond to the first small drift on the HSI rather than waiting for it to grow.
texts_at.3: SP flew the GPS computed course within about 3 degrees on every leg. The small residual came from a coordinated correction applied a moment after the deviation indicator first moved. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the correction the instant the deviation indicator moves, rather than a moment after.

texts_above.1: SP flew the heading called by the IP and stabilized on the computed course, with the error held to about 9 degrees before the oscillation stopped. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP responded to the first small drift on the HSI and re-established the computed course, holding the heading error to about 6.5 degrees throughout. Applying that correction the instant the indicator moves, rather than after a brief delay, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid heading and course tracking.
texts_above.3: SP flew the GPS computed course within about 3 degrees on every leg, with corrections small, coordinated and applied as soon as the course deviation moved. The technique is already sound; only the longest legs still call for the correction to be applied a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate course tracking.
texts_above.4: SP tracked the GPS computed course with the heading error inside about 1 degree throughout the route, anticipating drift corrections rather than reacting to them. The only refinement available was to log the anticipated drift for the debrief, since the tracking itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding course tracking precision.

error_modes.label: Programming of preplanned turning points and mission parameters

texts.0: SP, due to incomplete preflight preparation, did not program all preplanned turning points and the parameters necessary for mission execution into the GPS. Waypoints were missing or loaded out of sequence, and the displayed route did not match the briefed plan. The IP had to stop the sequence and rebuild the flight plan for the mission to continue.
texts.1: SP, due to rushed data entry on the ground, loaded the turning points with errors that surfaced only after engine start. The flight plan was corrected at the limit of the available time and only after the IP pointed out the discrepancies. SP did not verify the entries against the mission planning material.
texts.2: SP, due to omitting the readback of entered coordinates, loaded one turning point incorrectly. SP found the error during the self-check of the route legs and corrected it before taxi without IP involvement. Leg headings and total distance were then verified against the plan.
texts.3: SP programmed all preplanned turning points and the required parameters accurately and in the correct sequence. Each entry was verified against the planning material by leg course and distance. The loaded route matched the briefed plan with no further correction.
texts.4: SP loaded the complete route into the GPS quickly and without a single entry error. Verification was systematic, covering waypoint identifiers, leg courses, distances and total route length. The programmed plan was ready well before it was needed.
texts.marginal: SP produced a correct GPS flight plan but needed several attempts and more time than expected to complete the entries. Verification was performed once and covered distances but not leg courses. SP is expected to build a repeatable entry and check routine so that programming is complete and verified within normal planning time.

texts_at.0: With the IP pointing out each discrepancy against the mission planning material, SP corrected the flight plan entry named. Cross-checking the loaded waypoints against the mission planning material independently has not yet been asked of SP, so the programming still depends on the IP's call at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin naming one entry to verify before the IP points out a discrepancy, with the IP still confirming the remainder, before an independent programming check is required.
texts_at.1: SP corrected the flight plan with the discrepancies resolved before taxi, though the entries had needed a second review after engine start rather than one before it. The rushed entry traced to the mission planning material not being cross-checked against the loaded waypoints on the ground. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cross-check every entry against the mission planning material before engine start, not after it.
texts_at.2: SP found the incorrectly loaded turning point during the self-check of the route legs and corrected it before taxi. The omission traced to the readback of the entered coordinates being skipped on that one waypoint. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to read back every entered coordinate as it is typed, not only when the self-check is run afterward.
texts_at.3: SP programmed all preplanned turning points and the required parameters accurately, verifying each entry against the planning material by leg course and distance. The small residual came from a verification pass completed a minute later than the earliest point it could have started. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to start the verification pass as soon as the last waypoint is entered rather than a minute later.

texts_above.1: SP corrected the flight plan entry named by the IP, resolving the discrepancy against the mission planning material before taxi. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP found the single incorrectly loaded waypoint during the self-check of the route legs and corrected it before taxi, with every other entry verified by leg course and distance. Reading back each coordinate as it is typed, rather than relying on the later self-check alone, would remove even that one error. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady GPS programming discipline.
texts_above.3: SP programmed all preplanned turning points and the required parameters accurately and in the correct sequence, verifying each entry against the planning material by leg course and distance. The technique is already sound; only the busiest planning session still calls for the verification pass to start a moment sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed GPS programming technique.
texts_above.4: SP loaded the complete route into the GPS quickly and without a single entry error, verifying waypoint identifiers, leg courses, distances and total route length systematically. The only refinement available was to log the verification sequence used for the debrief, since the programming itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary GPS programming accuracy.

error_modes.label: Crosscheck of GPS data with other available navaids and map

texts.0: SP, due to a lapse in monitoring and crosschecking, accepted the GPS picture without comparing it with the VOR-DME/TACAN indications and the map. A gross position error went unrecognized and the aircraft was flown well off the planned route, holding a heading error beyond 10 degrees toward a wrong turning point. The IP had to intervene to re-establish the correct navigation.
texts.1: SP, due to weak monitoring of the other available navaids, made only one comparison of GPS data with the TACAN and the map during the whole leg. The mismatch was identified at the limit of usable time and only after the IP prompted the crosscheck. The route was regained, but the turning point was reached with a significant track offset.
texts.2: SP, due to concentrating on the GPS display, delayed the comparison with the TACAN and the map until midway through the leg. SP then detected the disagreement, resolved it against visual checkpoints and corrected a heading error of less than 10 degrees on its own initiative. The plan was maintained without IP input.
texts.3: SP crosschecked GPS data with the available navaids and the map on every leg. Position, bearing and distance were compared and agreed, and each small discrepancy was resolved immediately. Navigation stayed accurate with heading within 5 degrees of the computed course.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous and disciplined comparison of GPS information with TACAN, DME and visual map references. Each turning point was confirmed by at least two independent sources before the turn was started. No discrepancy was allowed to develop into a navigation error.
texts.marginal: SP performed the required crosscheck with the other navaids, but the comparison was routinely made after the turn rather than before it. The habit left little margin to catch a position error in time. SP is expected to complete the navaid and map comparison prior to each turning point, so that GPS data is confirmed rather than assumed.

texts_at.0: With the IP prompting the crosscheck against the TACAN and the map, SP compared the GPS picture once prompted. Comparing GPS data with the navaids and the map more than once on a leg, without a prompt, has not yet been asked of SP, so the crosscheck still depends on the IP's call at this stage. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin naming the TACAN indication before the IP prompts the comparison, with the IP still confirming the crosscheck, before an independent comparison is required.
texts_at.1: SP regained the route with the heading error at about 9 degrees before the crosscheck against the navaids was complete. The late comparison traced to only one crosscheck of GPS data against the TACAN and the map being made across the whole leg. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to compare GPS data against the navaids and the map more than once on every leg, not only near its end.
texts_at.2: SP detected the disagreement and resolved it against visual checkpoints, holding the heading correction under about 7 degrees on its own initiative. The delay traced to concentration on the GPS display before the comparison with the TACAN and the map was made. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make the navaid and map comparison at the midpoint of the leg by habit, not only when a discrepancy is suspected.
texts_at.3: SP crosschecked GPS data with the available navaids and the map on every leg, holding heading within about 3 degrees of the computed course. The small residual came from a discrepancy resolved a moment after it first appeared rather than in the same glance. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to resolve a small discrepancy in the same glance it appears, rather than a moment later.

texts_above.1: SP compared the GPS picture against the navaids once prompted by the IP, regaining the route with the heading error held to about 9 degrees. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP crosschecked GPS data against the TACAN and the map before a discrepancy could grow, holding heading within about 6.5 degrees of the computed course. Making that comparison at the midpoint of the leg by habit, rather than only when a discrepancy is suspected, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable navaid crosscheck technique.
texts_above.3: SP crosschecked GPS data with the available navaids and the map on every leg, with position, bearing and distance compared and agreeing and each small discrepancy resolved immediately, holding heading within about 3 degrees. The technique is already sound; only the busiest leg still calls for the comparison to be made a moment sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate navaid crosscheck discipline.
texts_above.4: SP maintained a continuous and disciplined comparison of GPS information with TACAN, DME and visual map references, confirming every turning point by at least two independent sources. The only refinement available was to log the sources used at each confirmation for the debrief, since the crosscheck itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional navaid crosscheck discipline.

error_modes.label: Knowledge and efficient use of GPS capabilities

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the GPS pages and functions, did not use the capabilities required by the mission. Basic operations such as direct-to routing, waypoint sequencing and data retrieval were attempted incorrectly or abandoned. The IP had to operate the equipment for the navigation task to be completed.
texts.1: SP, due to shallow familiarity with the menu structure, needed several attempts to reach the required GPS functions. The correct page was found only after the IP described the sequence. Navigation continued, but the delay disturbed the timing of the following leg.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation with a less frequently used GPS function, initially selected the wrong page. SP recognized the error, worked back through the menu and completed the intended operation in good time and without assistance. Mission timing was preserved.
texts.3: SP demonstrated good knowledge of the GPS and used its capabilities correctly and efficiently. Page selection, direct-to routing and data extraction were performed without hesitation. The equipment was used as a navigation aid at the pace the mission required.
texts.4: SP used the full range of GPS capabilities fluently and to the advantage of the mission. Functions were selected with no search time, including those beyond routine use. The equipment was handled as a well-understood tool rather than as an additional task.
texts.marginal: SP used the GPS correctly for routine functions but was noticeably slower whenever a less common capability was required. Knowledge was adequate without being consolidated across the full menu structure. SP is expected to practice the complete set of GPS functions so that all capabilities are available at operational speed.

texts_at.0: With the IP describing the menu sequence needed to reach the GPS function, SP worked through the sequence described. Recalling the full menu structure independently, without the sequence described, has not yet been asked of SP, so reaching a required function still depends on the IP's call at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin naming one step of the sequence before the IP describes it, with the IP still confirming the remainder, before independent recall is required.
texts_at.1: SP reached the required GPS function once the sequence was recalled, though the correct page had needed the sequence described before it could be found. The delay traced to shallow familiarity with the menu structure on the earliest attempt of the sortie. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to rehearse the full menu structure on the ground so the first attempt of the sortie does not need a description of the sequence.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the wrong page, worked back through the menu and completed the intended operation in good time. The hesitation traced to a less frequently used GPS function not being rehearsed as thoroughly as the routine ones. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to rehearse the less frequently used functions with the same repetition given to the routine ones.
texts_at.3: SP demonstrated good knowledge of the GPS and used its capabilities correctly and efficiently, with page selection, direct-to routing and data extraction performed without hesitation. The small residual came from a less common function that was located a moment slower than the routine ones. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring the less common functions up to the same recall speed as the routine ones.

texts_above.1: SP worked through the sequence described by the IP and reached the required GPS function, holding heading to within about 9 degrees of the assigned course, at the tolerance limit, before the following leg's timing was affected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP worked back through the menu without hesitation when a less frequent function was needed, completing the operation in good time and preserving the mission timing. Rehearsing that less frequent function to the same recall speed as the routine ones would remove the search step entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent GPS menu knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP demonstrated good knowledge of the GPS and used its capabilities correctly and efficiently, with page selection, direct-to routing and data extraction performed without hesitation. The technique is already sound; only the least common function still calls for a moment's more rehearsal to match the rest. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good GPS proficiency.
texts_above.4: SP used the full range of GPS capabilities fluently and to the advantage of the mission, with functions selected with no search time, including those beyond routine use. The only refinement available was to log which functions were used for the debrief, since the knowledge itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior GPS proficiency.

error_modes.label: Airborne GPS workload versus aircraft control priority

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on a single GPS entry problem, allowed the equipment task to capture the entire scan while airborne. Aircraft control and lookout lapsed, altitude departed by more than 300 feet and the aircraft continued past the turning point. The IP had to take over the navigation task to restore the flight profile.
texts.1: SP, due to fixation on the GPS while airborne, did not divide attention between the equipment and aircraft control. Altitude and heading deviations reached the limits of tolerance and were corrected only after the IP called for a return to the instruments. SP did not break the fixation without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an extended head-down period spent correcting a waypoint, briefly lost the priority of aircraft control. SP recognized the fixation, returned to the scan and corrected deviations that had stayed between the code 3 and code 1 zones. The GPS entry was then completed without further loss of control priority.
texts.3: SP kept the GPS workload subordinate to flying the aircraft. Head-down periods were short and deliberately broken by returns to the scan, so all parameters remained within the tighter limits. Equipment tasks were placed at points in the leg where workload allowed them.
texts.4: SP managed the airborne GPS workload with clear task prioritization. Entries were split into short blocks, each separated by a full instrument and outside scan, and no parameter moved appreciably. Aircraft control was never traded for equipment management.
texts.marginal: SP maintained control priority overall, but one unexpected GPS response held SP's attention longer than briefed before the scan was resumed. Standards were kept, although the margin narrowed during that period. SP is expected to set a fixed limit on head-down time and return to the scan before working the problem further.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for a return to the instruments while the GPS entry was worked, SP broke off the entry and returned to the scan on the call given. Setting a fixed limit on head-down time independently, without a call to return to the scan, has not yet been asked of SP, so control priority still depends on the IP's call at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin timing the head-down period independently, with the IP still calling the return to the scan, before independent control priority is required.
texts_at.1: SP returned to the scan with altitude at about 275 feet and airspeed at about 18 knots from the assigned values before the fixation was fully broken. The extended head-down period traced to a GPS entry problem that captured the scan on the earliest attempt to correct it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to set a fixed limit on head-down time from the first GPS problem of the sortie, not only after one has already run long.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the fixation, returned to the scan and corrected deviations that had stayed near about 210 feet and 14 knots of the assigned values. The extended period traced to a waypoint correction that ran longer than the briefed head-down limit. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to break off the waypoint correction at the briefed head-down limit even when the entry is not yet finished.
texts_at.3: SP kept the GPS workload subordinate to flying the aircraft, holding altitude to about 95 feet and airspeed to about 6 knots while doing so. The small residual came from a scan return completed a moment after the briefed limit on one entry. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to return to the scan at the briefed limit itself, not a moment after it.

texts_above.1: SP broke off the GPS entry and returned to the scan on the call from the IP, holding altitude to about 275 feet and airspeed to about 18 knots from the assigned values before the fixation was fully broken. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP set a fixed limit on head-down time and returned to the scan before it was reached, holding altitude to about 205 feet and airspeed to about 15 knots throughout the GPS work. Breaking off the entry at the briefed limit itself, even when unfinished, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady workload prioritization.
texts_above.3: SP kept the GPS workload subordinate to flying the aircraft, with head-down periods short and deliberately broken by returns to the scan, holding altitude within about 95 feet and airspeed within about 6 knots. The technique is already sound; only the most stubborn entry still calls for the break to be taken a moment sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined workload prioritization.
texts_above.4: SP managed the airborne GPS workload with clear task prioritization, splitting entries into short blocks each separated by a full instrument and outside scan, with no parameter moving appreciably. The only refinement available was to log the block lengths used for the debrief, since the prioritization itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate control priority under GPS workload.

error_modes.label: Independent navigation picture versus reliance on GPS

texts.0: SP, due to over-reliance on the GPS, navigated solely by the moving map and abandoned map reading and dead reckoning. When the displayed information did not match the ground picture, SP had no independent means of fixing position and continued toward a wrong feature. The IP had to intervene to re-establish orientation and regain the planned route.

The displayed course was followed with no raw data backup, the aircraft was flown off the planned track with a heading error beyond 10 degrees and the divergence went unrecognized. The IP had to intervene and re-establish the navigation on the radial and the DME distance.
texts.1: SP, due to treating the GPS as the primary navigation reference, tuned the VOR and DME only after being directed to and never identified the station by its ident. Raw data entered the crosscheck at the limit of usable time, with the track error already about 10 degrees off the computed course. texts.2: SP, due to working the GPS first and the navaids second, delayed tuning and identifying the VOR and DME for the leg. SP recognized that the advisory role of the equipment requires raw data backup, set the navaids up and confirmed the course while keeping the heading error under 10 degrees. error_modes.label: Groundspeed check for the effects of wind

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the groundspeed check after level off, never determined the effects of the winds on the route. texts.2: SP, due to a delayed groundspeed check, initially held the planned heading against outdated wind data. SP then read groundspeed from the GPS, compared it with the planned figure and revised the drift correction on its own initiative, keeping the heading error under 10 degrees. texts.3: SP accomplished a groundspeed check shortly after level off from the GPS readout and confirmed it with the DME change over one minute. Drift correction and ETAs were revised before any error could develop and the timing method was used to cross-confirm the GPS figure. Track and timing were maintained with negligible deviation.

error_modes.label: Fuel prediction at future points from actual fuel flow versus planned fuel

texts.0: SP, due to never combining groundspeed with the actual fuel flow on the EID, did not predict fuel at the future points of the route. Changes to the planned routing, altitude and winds were not recognized as drivers of a fuel difference and planned figures were quoted as if they were actual. Workload through the clearance, level off and descent phases was distributed so that no task competed with another.

texts.3: SP computed the desired start down point using the 2 to 1 ratio plus 10 miles and confirmed it against the GPS distance to go. The steepened gradient traced to the start down point being requested only after the distance to go had been pointed out. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to compute the start down point from the 2 to 1 ratio plus 10 miles before the distance to go needs to be pointed out.
texts_at.2: SP rechecked the figure against the GPS distance to go, corrected the request in good time and held the deviation to about 210 feet. The initial error traced to the 2 to 1 computation being made without the extra 10 miles for the approach. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to include the extra 10 miles for the approach in every 2 to 1 computation from the outset.
texts_at.3: SP computed the desired start down point using the 2 to 1 ratio plus 10 miles and confirmed it against the GPS distance to go, holding altitude within about 95 feet at the following fix. The small residual came from a confirmation check completed a moment after the request rather than before it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm the distance to go before requesting the descent rather than immediately after.

texts_above.1: SP requested the descent on the start down point called by the IP, regaining the planned altitude close to the fix with the deviation held to about 275 feet. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP rechecked the 2 to 1 computation against the GPS distance to go before requesting the descent, holding altitude to about 205 feet at the following fix. Confirming that distance before the request rather than immediately after would tighten the margin still further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound descent point computation.
texts_above.3: SP computed the desired start down point using the 2 to 1 ratio plus 10 miles and confirmed it against the GPS distance to go, holding altitude within about 95 feet and airspeed within about 6 knots of the plan. The technique is already sound; only the busiest descent still calls for the confirmation to be made a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise descent planning.
texts_above.4: SP had the start down point computed and cross-confirmed well before it was needed, requesting the descent to match the desired profile exactly with negligible deviation through the descent. The only refinement available was to log the exact computation for the debrief, since the descent planning itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding descent point computation.

error_modes.label: Temporary disorientation: climb to MSA until positive position is regained
error_modes.source: technique:8.20.3 MINIMUM SAFE ALTITUDE (MSA), EMERGENCY ROUTE ABORT ALTITUDE (ERAA) AND ROUTE ABORTS

texts.0: SP, due to temporary disorientation with regard to navigation, continued at the flown altitude instead of climbing to the MSA of the leg and kept searching the GPS display for a fix. Position was never positively regained and the aircraft was flown on with the route error beyond 10 degrees of heading. The IP had to intervene, initiate the climb and re-establish the position with the map and the navaids.
texts.1: SP, due to losing the position picture on the leg, delayed the climb to MSA and continued at low level while working the equipment. The climb was started only after the IP directed it and position was regained at the limit of usable time, with an altitude excursion of about 300 feet during the recovery. The distraction of low altitude flight was not recognized as a factor.
texts.2: SP, due to a temporary loss of the position picture, initially pressed on with the map and the GPS at the flown altitude. SP recognized the disorientation, climbed toward the MSA of the leg and regained a positive fix from the navaids in good time, holding the intermediate deviation bands throughout. No IP input was required.
texts.3: SP recognized the doubt about position immediately and climbed to the MSA of the leg while re-establishing the fix with the map, the GPS and the navaids. Altitude was held within 150 feet of the MSA during the recovery and the route was rejoined once position was positive. The sequence of climb first and navigate second was followed.
texts.4: SP never allowed the position picture to lapse and, at the first ambiguity, climbed at once toward the MSA with the fix re-established from independent sources before the climb was complete. Aircraft control through the climb showed negligible deviation. The MSA of each leg and the ERAA of the route were available from memory at any moment.
texts.marginal: SP recovered the position within standards, but the climb toward the MSA was started only after two attempts to resolve the doubt on the GPS. The habit places the equipment ahead of terrain clearance when position is uncertain. SP is expected to climb to the MSA first and regain the fix afterwards, since low altitude flight increases distraction and complicates the recovery.

texts_at.0: With the IP directing the climb to MSA and re-establishing the fix, SP flew the climb directed. Recognizing low altitude flight as a distraction and climbing toward the MSA independently has not yet been asked of SP, so the recovery still depends on the IP's call at this stage. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin stating the doubt about position before the IP directs the climb, with the IP still re-establishing the fix, before an independent recovery is required.
texts_at.1: SP climbed toward the MSA with the altitude excursion at about 275 feet during the recovery before position was regained. The delay traced to low altitude flight not being recognized as a distraction while the equipment was worked first. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to recognize low altitude flight as a distraction and to climb toward the MSA as soon as the position picture is lost, not after the equipment has been worked first.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the disorientation, climbed toward the MSA of the leg and regained a positive fix from the navaids in good time, holding the excursion to about 210 feet during the climb. The initial delay traced to the map and the GPS being pressed at the flown altitude before the climb was started. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to start the climb toward the MSA before working the map and the GPS, not alongside them.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the doubt about position immediately and climbed to the MSA of the leg while re-establishing the fix, holding altitude within about 95 feet of the MSA during the recovery. The small residual came from a fix confirmed a moment after the climb was already under way rather than at its start. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to begin re-establishing the fix at the same moment the climb starts, not a moment later.

texts_above.1: SP flew the climb directed by the IP, holding the altitude excursion to about 275 feet during the recovery before position was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the disorientation and climbed toward the MSA of the leg before working the map and the GPS, holding the excursion to about 205 feet during the recovery. Beginning the fix re-establishment at the same moment the climb starts, rather than a moment later, would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured MSA climb discipline.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the doubt about position immediately and climbed to the MSA of the leg while re-establishing the fix with the map, the GPS and the navaids, holding altitude within about 95 feet of the MSA during the recovery. The technique is already sound; only the earliest recognition of doubt still calls for the climb to begin a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined MSA climb technique.
texts_above.4: SP never allowed the position picture to lapse and, at the first ambiguity, climbed at once toward the MSA with the fix re-established from independent sources before the climb was complete, with negligible deviation through the climb. The only refinement available was to log the exact ambiguity that triggered the climb for the debrief, since the recovery itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate MSA climb discipline.
